## Problem 1

```{r}
bday_sim = function(n) {
  
  bdays = sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  
  duplicate = length(unique(bdays)) < n
  
  return(duplicate)
  
}
```
```{r}
bday_results = 
  expand_grid(
    group_size = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |> 
  mutate(has_duplicate = map_lgl(group_size, bday_sim)) |> 
  group_by(group_size) |> 
  summarize(prob_shared = mean(has_duplicate))
```
```{r}
bday_results |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = prob_shared)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_point(alpha = .5) + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") + 
  labs(
    title = "Probability of at least one shared birthday, by group size",
    x = "Group size",
    y = "Probability of a shared birthday",
    caption = "10,000 simulations per group size")
```

The probability of at least one shared birthday increases steadily with group size, following an S-shaped curve. The probability is very small for groups of fewer than ten people, rises steeply between roughly 15 and 35, and then flattens as it approaches one. With 23 people the probability is `r bday_results |> filter(group_size == 23) |> pull(prob_shared) |> round(3)`, crossing 50% at a group size most people find surprisingly small; by 50 people it reaches `r bday_results |> filter(group_size == 50) |> pull(prob_shared) |> round(3)`. The result is counterintuitive because people tend to think about how many others share *their own* birthday rather than how many pairs exist in the group. A group of 23 contains 253 distinct pairs, and only one of them needs to match.

## Problem 2

```{r, warning = FALSE}
study_df = 
  tibble(
    file_name = list.files("./data/data")
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    data = map(file_name, \(x) read_csv(str_c("./data/data/", x), show_col_types = FALSE)),
    subject = str_remove(file_name, ".csv")
  ) |> 
  unnest(data) |> 
  separate(subject, into = c("arm", "subject_id"), sep = "_", remove = FALSE) |> 
  mutate(
    arm = case_match(arm, "con" ~ "Control", "exp" ~ "Experimental"),
    arm = factor(arm, levels = c("Control", "Experimental"))
  ) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    week_1:week_8,
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |> 
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week)) |> 
  select(subject, arm, subject_id, week, value)

study_df
```
```{r}
study_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = value, color = arm, group = subject)) + 
  geom_line(alpha = .6) + 
  geom_point(alpha = .4, size = 1) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) + 
  labs(
    title = "Observations on each subject over time, by study arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observed value",
    color = "Study arm")
```

```{r}
week_means = 
  study_df |> 
  filter(week %in% c(1, 8)) |> 
  group_by(arm, week) |> 
  summarize(mean_value = mean(value), .groups = "drop")

week_means |> knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

At week 1 the two arms are indistinguishable. Group means are nearly identical (`r week_means |> filter(arm == "Control", week == 1) |> pull(mean_value) |> round(2)` in the control arm and `r week_means |> filter(arm == "Experimental", week == 1) |> pull(mean_value) |> round(2)` in the experimental arm), and individual trajectories are fully intermingled. Over the following weeks the experimental arm trends upward while the control arm stays flat, ending at `r week_means |> filter(arm == "Experimental", week == 8) |> pull(mean_value) |> round(2)` and `r week_means |> filter(arm == "Control", week == 8) |> pull(mean_value) |> round(2)` respectively. By week 8 the groups have almost completely separated: nearly every experimental subject sits above nearly every control subject. Both arms show substantial week-to-week variability within individual subjects, so single observations are noisy; the difference between groups appears in the trend across weeks rather than in any one measurement.
